processing: A strip-shaped baked green made partly by hand and partly by machine in six stages: pan-fixing, rolling, shaping, baking, sorting and a final firing.
harvest_season: One bud with one open leaf up to one bud with two half-open leaves. The season is not stated; as with other Yunnan greens, spring is the usual prized picking.
appearance_dry: Tight, fine strips with plenty of down from the large-leaf buds.
taste_profile: Fresh and full yet mellow, with an aroma that holds even as the cup cools and a lingering sweet finish.

brewing.notes: General advice for downy Yunnan greens: water a little off the boil. Smell the cup again when it cools, because the aroma is known for lasting.

vintage_note: A green tea sold as the current year's picking, as is usual for its class, and best within about a year. It comes in three grades in descending order: Huafo Longzhua, Huafo Cha and Huafo Xiangming. In the narrow sense the name means only the middle one.
description:
Huafo tea is a modern Yunnan green from the Qingfeng tea farm in Mouding county, Chuxiong. The farm sits at 1,968 metres next to Huafo Mountain, with the county's largest reservoir below it.

It is made from the Mengku large-leaf variety of Shuangjiang, which gives the leaf its heavy down. The pan-fixing runs hot at first and then cooler, tender leaf getting a longer fix and older leaf a shorter one, and short rolling keeps the sharp tips whole. Baking and a final firing finish it.

The cup is clear green, with a fresh and full flavour that stays mellow. Its known trait is an aroma that lasts as it cools, so it is worth tasting slowly. Large-leaf tea can bite, so keep the water just off the boil and the steeps short.

When buying, look for the grade. Huafo Longzhua is the top of the range, Huafo Cha the standard and Huafo Xiangming the everyday quality green.
history:
Huafo is a recent creation, developed in 1982. That same year it was named a large-leaf white-down famous tea at a Yunnan provincial appraisal of fine cultivars and famous teas.

It was sold mainly to cities such as Kunming, Shanghai and Beijing. The name comes from the neighbouring Huafo Mountain, not from any old tea tradition.
